messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Vignette:
Ethan was 21, a married European-American social ministry worker, and when he first came for help he spoke in the careful, restrained way of someone who had spent months trying not to let his mind return to one particular place. Before the war, his life had been straightforward and ordinary: he and his wife had been building a shared routine, and his work had taken him into a relief role that he had once experienced as meaningful and concrete. That changed after he was sent into a war zone to support civilians, where the daily atmosphere was shaped by military presence, fear, and the constant possibility that something could erupt without warning. The event that still sat at the center of his distress occurred during one of those shifts when he was moving through an area affected by fighting and heard shouting in Arabic nearby. At the time, the language itself did not matter to him in any abstract sense; what mattered was the force of it, the urgency and volume, and the fact that it came when the situation already felt unstable. In that moment, and in the moments that followed, he experienced the event as overwhelming and extreme. Even now he said that part of what unsettled him most was that the memory felt almost too severe to believe had actually happened to him.

After returning home, Ethan found that the event did not stay in the past in the way other memories did. When people talked about the military, even casually, he felt his attention snap toward the conversation as if something in him had to check what was being said. Talking about the event itself was even harder; if he was asked about it directly, he could feel the same terror return with surprising force, and he often described the memory as if it were happening right in front of him rather than something that had ended. He would sit rigidly, trying to keep his face composed, but inside he felt pulled back into the scene with an intensity that unsettled him. The memory was not just vivid; it had a quality of immediacy that made distance feel unavailable. He did not describe it as an abstract recollection, but as something that could take hold of him again in the present tense.

In the months that followed, Ethan began arranging his evenings so he could stay up until very late. He said that going to bed early left him alone with the possibility of waking in the night, and he had become accustomed to rousing himself to check whether he was safe. These checks were brief but repeated, and he treated them as necessary, something he had to do before he could settle again. At work, where he continued in social ministry, he noticed that strangers approaching him in ordinary settings could make him feel threatened, even if nothing about the moment objectively suggested danger. This was especially noticeable in the kinds of public-facing spaces his job required, where he might be expected to speak with unfamiliar people or move among groups in the community. He also found himself becoming immediately on guard when people made sudden movements around him. A quick turn, an unexpected step, or an abrupt gesture was enough to sharpen his body’s alertness and leave him scanning the space around him, waiting for what might happen next.

Ethan had also started avoiding anything that might leave him feeling happy or hopeful. He described this in an almost embarrassed way, as though it made little sense on paper, but for him those moments carried a risk he could not ignore. Positive feelings seemed to expose how much he had lost and how far removed he felt from who he had been before the war. He often chose to postpone anything uplifting, keeping himself from celebrations or from sitting too long in enjoyable company. Alongside this, he spent a great deal of time ruminating about how the event could have been prevented. He replayed decisions, sequences, and possibilities, looking for the point at which he might have done something differently. The thinking did not bring him closure, but it was persistent, and it was tied to a wish to understand whether the horror had been avoidable. His wife had noticed that he was less present in shared moments, and he admitted that even when he was with her, part of him was elsewhere, circling back to the same questions.

What finally brought Ethan to treatment was the cumulative strain of living as though the war could re-enter at any moment, even in ordinary American settings. He was increasingly worn down by the nights, the vigilance, the way conversations about the military or the event itself could pull him straight back into that place, and the sense that his own life had become narrower around what he was trying not to feel. He came hoping that he would no longer be dragged so completely into the memory, and that he might sleep without repeatedly checking the darkness. More than anything, he was afraid that the terror would keep feeling present forever, and that the parts of life he had been avoiding would remain out of reach.
